verdict.reasoning: Patient states chest has been tight for about three hours: 'My chest has been feeling really tight.' and 'About three hours now.'

Patient reports mild shortness of breath, wheeze, and slight cough: 'Yeah, like a little bit. Yeah, a little bit short of breath. Not too bad.' and 'Yeah, I'm feeling a bit wheezy as well.' and 'Yeah, Slight cough.' The doctor later summarizes it as a nonproductive cough: 'it's non productive cough' and patient confirms no sputum: 'Are you coughing up anything?' 'No.'

Cough has persisted after a recent cold and is a bit worse at night: 'You know, I had a cold last week... The coughs kind of stuck around.' and 'Is the cough worse at nighttime?' 'I mean it gets a little bit worse at night, but basically just pretty consistent.'
Recent URI last week with sore throat and runny nose, improving nasal symptoms: 'I had a cold last week... I had a sore throat, I had a runny nose.' and 'the runny nose isn't as bad anymore.'

Patient denies chest pain and describes tightness and difficulty taking full breath: Doctor: 'you wouldn't say you've got chest pain. It's more a tight chest, is it?' Patient: 'No, not really pain, it's more like tight. It just feels like sometimes you can't get a full breath in, you know?'

Not short of breath at rest but more on stairs: 'Definitely not short of breath at rest... It does. When I'm walking upstairs, I do feel like I have a little bit more short of breath than I would normally be.' and doctor confirms: 'but you're not short of breath of rest at the moment?' 'No, no, no, I'm not.'

History of prior severe asthma exacerbation in high school requiring intubation and inpatient stay: 'when I was in high school I had to have a tube put down my throat.' and doctor: 'you stayed in hospital for a few days, did you? With an asthma exacerbation?' Patient: 'Yeah, I did, yeah.'
Patient confirms asthma: Doctor: 'any other medical problems, like asthma?' Patient: 'Yeah, yeah, I have asthma. I've had it for a while now.'
Patient mentions hay fever/allergies: 'And then I have, like, a hay fever, you know, some allergies.'
History of childhood eczema: 'When I was young I also had eczema...'
History of childhood milk protein allergy: 'When I was young I also had eczema and I had a milk protein allergy when I was young too.'
Patient uses Salbutamol (Ventolin): 'Yeah, so, you know the Ventolin, it's called Salbutamol. Yeah, I got that one.'

Patient was using a steroid inhaler ('clinol') but ran out about a week ago and is not currently using it: 'then I have a steroid. Clinol inhaler.' and 'I forgot to bring it with me, so I haven't really in the past week because... They ran out and I forgot to go and grab the next one.' and doctor: 'So you haven't got any clinical or any Ventolin at the moment?' Patient: 'Not with me right now. No, I ran out.'
No known drug allergies: Doctor: 'Any drug allergies that you know of?' Patient: 'No, no, not allergic to anything. Just like. Just the dust and stuff, but nothing. No drugs.'
Environmental allergy to dust: 'Just like. Just the dust and stuff, but nothing. No drugs.'
Mother has eczema: 'Yeah, my mom has eczema...'
Father has asthma: '...and my dad has asthma.'

Transcript supports all elements: recent cold/viral URI, lapse in inhalers for about a week, three hours of chest tightness, mild SOB and wheeze, dry (nonproductive) cough, no SOB at rest, and prior severe exacerbation with intubation and admission. Doctor also frames current episode as 'this asthma attack' and prescribes asthma-directed therapy, supporting assessment of asthma exacerbation.
Plan to prescribe Ventolin: 'I would quite like to certainly get you some Ventolin clinomodulate.' and later: 'What I like to do is send you these. Some prescriptions for your inhalers are ongoing.'

Plan to prescribe steroid inhaler similar to prior 'clinol': 'I would quite like to certainly get you some Ventolin clinomodulate.' and 'Once you get better from this asthma attack, you can. You can use the clinalmodulate in the morning...' indicating re-prescribing his controller steroid inhaler.

Plan for oral steroids for five days, two tablets each morning: 'I think the other thing I'd like to do is just give you a dose of steroids. So these are tablets which you can take for five days, two tablets in the morning...'
Plan to provide a spacer: 'And the other thing I'd like to send you is a spacer which would allow the medication to actually go into your lungs.'
'Use inhaled corticosteroids daily in the morning' matches: 'you can. Once you get better from this asthma attack, you can. You can use the clinalmodulate in the morning...'
Instruction to use SABA as needed: 'with Ventolin as a prn. So Ventolin when you need to.'
Spacer teaching details: 'it has some instructions about how to use it, but essentially couple of puffs to prime it inside, breathing in and out for five or ten breaths.'

Safety-net on SABA use and symptom worsening: 'If you should start to use the Ventolin more than every three hours at any time, it's a good idea to seek medical attention...' and 'Any deterioration in your symptoms, like worsening shortness of breath or just generally concerning symptoms, pain in your chest, tightness, feeling lightheaded, then seek further medical attention anytime, please.'

Advice re rest and self-certifying: 'And might give you some time off work as well. You can self certify for seven days, but I think I would advise you just to rest a little bit until you're feeling a bit better...'
